questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Regional Aspirations and Conflicts
questions.sub_topic: Punjab and North-East milestones
questions.question:
Match List-I (Event) with List-II (Year).

List-I
(A) Anandpur Sahib Resolution
(B) Operation Blue Star
(C) Rajiv Gandhi–Longowal Accord
(D) Mizo Accord with Laldenga

List-II
(I) 1986
(II) 1985
(III) 1984
(IV) 1973
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Why: The Akali Dal passed the Anandpur Sahib Resolution in 1973 (IV). Operation Blue Star took place in the Golden Temple in June 1984 (III). The Rajiv Gandhi–Longowal Accord was signed in July 1985 (II). The Mizo Accord with Laldenga was signed in 1986 (I).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps 1984 and 1985. Option (C) puts the resolution after Blue Star. Option (D) swaps the two accords.
Key point: Punjab 1973–85 and Mizoram 1986 show conflict ending in accords.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Politics of Planned Development
questions.sub_topic: Industrialists' joint proposal for a planned economy
questions.question: In 1944 a section of the big industrialists got together and drafted a joint proposal for setting up a planned economy in the country. It came to be called the:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Bombay Plan
Why: The Bombay Plan of 1944 was drafted by leading industrialists. It wanted the state to take major initiatives in industrial and other economic investment, which shows that planning had wide support.
Why not the others:
(B) The People's Plan came from the labour leader M.N. Roy.
(C) The Gandhian Plan was S.N. Agarwal's decentralised alternative.
(D) The Sarvodaya Plan was J.P. Narayan's later proposal.
Key point: Even big business backed planning before Independence.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Regional Aspirations and Conflicts
questions.sub_topic: State that was NOT carved out of Assam
questions.question: Several States of the North-East were carved out of the old State of Assam after Independence. Which of the following was NOT one of them?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Tripura
Why: Tripura, like Manipur, was a princely state that merged with India after Independence; it was never part of Assam.
Why not the others:
(B) Nagaland became a State in 1963.
(C) Meghalaya was carved out in 1972.
(D) Mizoram became a Union Territory in 1972 and a State in 1987.
Key point: Tripura and Manipur were princely states; the rest grew out of Assam.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Environment and Natural Resources in Global Politics
questions.sub_topic: Environmental agreements and their years
questions.question:
Match List-I (Agreement or conference) with List-II (Year).

List-I
(A) Antarctic Treaty
(B) Montreal Protocol
(C) Earth Summit at Rio de Janeiro
(D) Kyoto Protocol

List-II
(I) 1987
(II) 1959
(III) 1992
(IV) 1997
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
Why: The Antarctic Treaty was signed in 1959 (II). The Montreal Protocol on the ozone layer came in 1987 (I). The Earth Summit was held at Rio in 1992 (III). The Kyoto Protocol was agreed in 1997 (IV).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps 1959 and 1987. Option (B) puts Montreal at 1992. Option (C) swaps Rio and Kyoto.
Key point: The global commons are protected through 1959, 1987, 1992 and 1997 milestones.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Globalisation and Its Critics
questions.sub_topic: Globalisation and its critics — the false claim
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Globalisation involves flows of ideas, capital, commodities and people across the world.
(B) Some fear that globalisation leads to cultural homogenisation, sometimes called McDonaldisation.
(C) The first meeting of the World Social Forum was held at Porto Alegre in 2001.
(D) India began its economic reforms and opened its economy in 1981.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (D) only
Why: Only (D) is false: India began its economic reforms in 1991, in response to a financial crisis.
Why not the others: (A) these four flows define globalisation. (B) critics fear that one dominant culture, mostly Western, will spread everywhere. (C) the World Social Forum first met in Brazil in 2001. Options (A), (B) and (C) name a true statement as false.
Key point: Globalisation is multi-dimensional, and India's turn came in 1991.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Era of One-Party Dominance
questions.sub_topic: Why Congress won far more seats than its vote share in 1952
questions.question: In the first general election Congress won about 45 per cent of the votes but 364 of the 489 seats. Why did it win so many more seats than its vote share suggests?
options: A) It won many seats with under half the votes, under first-past-the-post.
B) Most opposition parties boycotted the election in the majority of States.
C) Lok Sabha seats were allotted to parties in proportion to their votes.
D) Only Congress candidates could contest from the reserved constituencies.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) It won many seats with under half the votes, under first-past-the-post.
Why: Under first-past-the-post, the candidate with the most votes wins even without a majority. With the opposition divided, Congress won many seats with under 50 per cent of the vote.
Why not the others:
(B) There was no boycott; the Socialists, Communists and Jana Sangh contested.
(C) Proportional representation is not used for the Lok Sabha.
(D) Reserved seats were open to candidates of any party.
Key point: A divided opposition plus first-past-the-post magnified Congress's lead.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: South Asia in the Post-Cold War Era
questions.sub_topic: Democracy and cooperation in South Asia — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) SAARC was set up in 1985.
(B) The SAFTA agreement was signed in 2004.
(C) In 2005 the Maldives' parliament voted to introduce a multi-party system.
(D) Nepal's monarchy was abolished in 1990.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) SAARC was set up in 1985. (B) SAFTA was signed at the 2004 summit and came into force in 2006. (C) the Maldives moved to a multi-party system in 2005.
Why not the others: (D) is false: in 1990 the king accepted a democratic constitution but kept the monarchy; Nepal's monarchy was abolished in 2008. Options (C) and (D) include (D); option (A) leaves out (C).
Key point: Nepal restored democracy in 1990 and became a republic in 2008.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: Country of Secretary-General Kofi Annan
questions.question: Kofi Annan, UN Secretary-General from 1997 to 2006, was from:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Ghana
Why: Kofi Annan, a Ghanaian diplomat, was the seventh Secretary-General. He started reform efforts at the UN.
Why not the others:
(A) Egypt's Boutros Boutros-Ghali was his predecessor.
(C) Peru's Javier Pérez de Cuéllar served before Boutros-Ghali.
(D) South Korea's Ban Ki-moon succeeded Annan.
Key point: Pérez de Cuéllar → Boutros-Ghali → Annan → Ban Ki-moon.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Challenge to and Restoration of Congress System
questions.sub_topic: Congress after Nehru — the false claim
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) After Shastri's death in 1966, Indira Gandhi became Prime Minister.
(B) Under the Kamaraj Plan of 1963, senior Congress leaders resigned from office to work for the party.
(C) In the 1967 elections the Congress lost its majority in the Lok Sabha.
(D) In 1967 the Congress lost power in several States to non-Congress coalitions.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C) only
Why: Only (C) is false: the Congress kept a narrow majority in the Lok Sabha in 1967. Its tally fell sharply, to its lowest till then.
Why not the others: (A) Indira Gandhi was chosen as Prime Minister in January 1966. (B) the Kamaraj Plan asked senior ministers to resign and rebuild the party. (D) non-Congress coalitions came to power in several States. Options (A), (B) and (D) name a true statement as false.
Key point: 1967 was an "earthquake" in the States, not a loss of the Centre.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: India's External Relations
questions.sub_topic: Agreements and conferences of India's foreign policy
questions.question:
Match List-I (Event) with List-II (Year).

List-I
(A) Panchsheel agreement between India and China
(B) Afro-Asian conference at Bandung
(C) Tashkent Agreement between India and Pakistan
(D) Shimla Agreement between India and Pakistan

List-II
(I) 1966
(II) 1954
(III) 1972
(IV) 1955
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)
Why: Panchsheel was signed by Nehru and Zhou Enlai on 29 April 1954 (II). The Bandung conference was held in Indonesia in 1955 (IV). The Tashkent Agreement, signed in January 1966, ended the 1965 war (I). The Shimla Agreement was signed in July 1972, after the 1971 war (III).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps Panchsheel and Bandung. Option (B) swaps the two India–Pakistan agreements. Option (C) puts Bandung after the Tashkent Agreement.
Key point: Tashkent closed the 1965 war; Shimla closed the 1971 war.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: What four international bodies do
questions.question:
Match List-I (Organisation) with List-II (Main role).

List-I
(A) International Monetary Fund
(B) World Bank
(C) World Trade Organisation
(D) International Atomic Energy Agency

List-II
(I) Promotes the peaceful use of nuclear energy
(II) Sets the rules for global trade
(III) Oversees financial institutions and regulations at the international level
(IV) Gives loans and grants for human development, agriculture and infrastructure
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Why: The IMF oversees international financial institutions and regulations (III). The World Bank gives loans and grants to developing countries (IV). The WTO, set up in 1995, sets the rules of global trade (II). The IAEA, set up in 1957, promotes the peaceful use of nuclear energy (I).
Why not the others: Option (B) swaps the IMF and the World Bank. Option (C) swaps the World Bank and the WTO. Option (D) swaps the WTO and the IAEA.
Key point: The Bretton Woods twins are the IMF (finance) and the World Bank (development lending).

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: India's External Relations
questions.sub_topic: Defence minister who resigned after the 1962 war
questions.question: Which Defence Minister had to resign after India's reverses in the 1962 war with China?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) V.K. Krishna Menon
Why: After the defeat of 1962, there was strong criticism of the government. V.K. Krishna Menon left the cabinet, and Nehru's own standing suffered.
Why not the others:
(A) Y.B. Chavan succeeded Menon as Defence Minister.
(B) Swaran Singh was Foreign Minister and later Defence Minister.
(D) Jagjivan Ram was Defence Minister during the 1971 war.
Key point: 1962 cost Krishna Menon his post.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Environment and Natural Resources in Global Politics
questions.sub_topic: Sacred groves as an example of resources
questions.question: Sacred groves, protected by communities in many parts of India, are an example of:
options: A) private property owned by individuals
B) global commons outside any state's control
C) common property resources managed by a community
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) common property resources managed by a community
Why: Common property resources are owned and used by a group or community, which keeps rules for their use. Sacred groves are managed this way.
Why not the others:
(A) No single individual owns a sacred grove.
(B) The global commons, such as the high seas and Antarctica, lie outside any state.
(D) Reserved forests are managed by the state, not by community custom.
Key point: Common property is shared by a community, not by the world.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Environment and Natural Resources in Global Politics
questions.sub_topic: Source of the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities
questions.question: The principle of "common but differentiated responsibilities" in environmental matters was set out in:
options: D) the Stockholm Declaration on human rights
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) the Rio Declaration of 1992
Why: The Rio Declaration of 1992 stated that states have common but differentiated responsibilities. Developed countries bear a special responsibility because of the pressure their societies put on the environment.
Why not the others:
(B) The Antarctic Treaty keeps that region for peaceful, scientific use.
(C) The Montreal Protocol limits ozone-depleting substances.
(D) No such human rights declaration set out this principle.
Key point: India relies on this principle in climate negotiations.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Democratic Upsurge and Coalition Politics
questions.sub_topic: The Mandal Commission — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The Second Backward Classes Commission, known as the Mandal Commission, was appointed by the Janata Party government.
(B) It was headed by B.P. Mandal.
(C) It recommended reserving 27 per cent of seats in educational institutions and government jobs for the backward classes.
(D) Its recommendations on jobs were implemented by the P.V. Narasimha Rao government in 1990.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) the Janata Party government set up the Commission. (B) B.P. Mandal headed it. (C) it recommended 27 per cent reservation for the backward classes.
Why not the others: (D) is false: the National Front government of V.P. Singh decided in August 1990 to implement the recommendations. Options (B) and (D) include (D); option (A) leaves out (C).
Key point: Appointed by the Janata government, implemented by V.P. Singh in 1990.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: South Asia in the Post-Cold War Era
questions.sub_topic: Agreement under which the IPKF went to Sri Lanka
questions.question: The Indian Peace Keeping Force (IPKF) was sent to Sri Lanka in 1987 under:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) the India–Sri Lanka Accord
Why: In 1987 India and Sri Lanka signed an accord, and India sent the IPKF to help stabilise relations between the government and the Tamils. It was pulled out in 1989.
Why not the others:
(A) The Shimla Agreement was with Pakistan in 1972.
(B) The Farakka Agreement concerned Ganga waters with Bangladesh.
(D) Panchsheel was signed with China in 1954.
Key point: IPKF, 1987–89, came out of the India–Sri Lanka Accord.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: Last years of the Soviet bloc in order
questions.question:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
(A) The fall of the Berlin Wall
(B) Gorbachev becomes General Secretary of the Soviet Communist Party
(C) The disintegration of the Soviet Union
(D) Lithuania declares independence from the USSR
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (B), (A), (D), (C)
Why: (B) Gorbachev took over in March 1985. (A) The Berlin Wall fell in November 1989. (D) Lithuania declared independence in March 1990. (C) The USSR was dissolved in December 1991.
Why not the others: Option (A) puts Lithuania before the Berlin Wall. Option (B) puts the Berlin Wall before Gorbachev. Option (D) puts the end of the USSR before Lithuania's declaration.
Key point: Reform from 1985 led to collapse by 1991.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Challenge to and Restoration of Congress System
questions.sub_topic: Origin of the phrase 'Aya Ram, Gaya Ram'
questions.question: The phrase 'Aya Ram, Gaya Ram', used for frequent defections, came from the case of an MLA who changed his party three times within a fortnight in 1967. Which State was he from?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Haryana
Why: Gaya Lal, an MLA in Haryana, changed parties three times in a fortnight in 1967. The phrase became shorthand for defection.
Why not the others:
(B), (C), (D) Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Punjab also had unstable coalition governments after 1967, but the phrase comes from Gaya Lal of Haryana.
Key point: Defection politics grew out of the post-1967 coalitions.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: Size of the UN Security Council
questions.question: How many members does the UN Security Council have?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 15
Why: The Security Council has 15 members: 5 permanent members with a veto, and 10 non-permanent members elected for two-year terms.
Why not the others:
(A) 5 is only the permanent members.
(B) 10 is only the non-permanent members.
(D) 193 is the membership of the General Assembly.
Key point: 5 permanent + 10 elected = 15.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Democratic Upsurge and Coalition Politics
questions.sub_topic: Governments at the Centre from 1989 to 2004 in order
questions.question:
Arrange these governments at the Centre in the order in which they first took office:
(A) The United Front government
(B) The National Front government
(C) The NDA government led by Atal Bihari Vajpayee
(D) The UPA government led by Manmohan Singh
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (B), (A), (C), (D)
Why: (B) The National Front, under V.P. Singh, took office in December 1989. (A) The United Front, under H.D. Deve Gowda, followed in June 1996. (C) Vajpayee's NDA came in March 1998. (D) The UPA, under Manmohan Singh, came in May 2004.
Why not the others: Option (A) puts the United Front first. Option (C) puts the NDA before the United Front. Option (D) puts the National Front after the NDA.
Key point: 1989 → 1996 → 1998 → 2004 was the era of coalitions.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Era of One-Party Dominance
questions.sub_topic: Leaders of the early opposition parties
questions.question:
Match List-I (Leader) with List-II (Party).

List-I
(A) Acharya Narendra Dev
(B) C. Rajagopalachari
(C) Deen Dayal Upadhyaya
(D) A.K. Gopalan

List-II
(I) Swatantra Party
(II) Communist Party of India
(III) Socialist Party
(IV) Bharatiya Jana Sangh
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)
Why: Acharya Narendra Dev was a founder of the Socialist Party (III). Rajagopalachari founded the Swatantra Party in 1959 (I). Deen Dayal Upadhyaya led the Bharatiya Jana Sangh (IV). A.K. Gopalan was a Communist leader from Kerala (II).
Why not the others: Option (A) gives Rajagopalachari to the Jana Sangh; he was a former Congressman who founded the pro-market Swatantra Party. Option (C) swaps the Socialist and Communist leaders. Option (D) swaps Narendra Dev and Upadhyaya.
Key point: Socialists, Communists, Jana Sangh and Swatantra were the main early opposition parties.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Nation-Building and Its Problems
questions.sub_topic: First part of India to hold an election under universal adult franchise
questions.question: Which part of India became the first to hold an election under universal adult franchise, in June 1948, before the Constitution came into force?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Manipur
Why: Just before Independence, the Maharaja of Manipur, Bodhachandra Singh, agreed to a democratic set-up for his State. Elections were held in June 1948 under universal adult franchise, making Manipur a constitutional monarchy.
Why not the others:
(A) Hyderabad was integrated after police action in September 1948.
(B) Travancore merged into the Travancore-Cochin union.
(C) Junagadh was integrated after a plebiscite.
Key point: Manipur held India's first universal-franchise election, in 1948.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: Asian G-7 member that suffered nuclear destruction
questions.question: Which Asian country is a member of the G-7 and the only country to have suffered the destruction caused by nuclear bombs?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Japan
Why: Japan is the only Asian member of the G-7. Hiroshima and Nagasaki were bombed in 1945.
Why not the others:
(A) China is not a G-7 member.
(C) South Korea is not a G-7 member.
(D) India is not a G-7 member.
Key point: Japan is an economic power that keeps its defence spending low.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Security in the Contemporary World
questions.sub_topic: People displaced within their own country
questions.question: People who have been forced to leave their homes but remain within their own country's borders are called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) internally displaced persons
Why: Internally displaced persons have fled their homes but not crossed an international border; refugees have crossed one.
Why not the others:
(A) Refugees leave their own country.
(C) Migrant workers move for work, usually by choice.
(D) Asylum seekers ask another country for protection.
Key point: Crossing a border is what separates refugees from IDPs.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Regional Aspirations and Conflicts
questions.sub_topic: Organisation that led the Assam movement of 1979–85
questions.question: The movement against 'outsiders' in Assam from 1979 to 1985 was led by:
options: D) the All Assam Students' Union
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) the All Assam Students' Union
Why: The All Assam Students' Union (AASU) led the movement against illegal migrants. It ended with the Assam Accord of 1985, after which its leaders formed the Asom Gana Parishad.
Why not the others:
(A) The Mizo National Front led the Mizo struggle under Laldenga.
(B) The Naga National Council was led by Phizo.
(C) The Asom Gana Parishad was formed after the movement ended, in 1985.
Key point: AASU led the agitation; AGP was its political successor.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Politics of Planned Development
questions.sub_topic: Main focus of the First Five Year Plan
questions.question: Which sector did the First Five Year Plan (1951–56) focus on most?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Agriculture
Why: The First Plan aimed mainly to get the country out of poverty. It put the greatest weight on agriculture, investing in dams and irrigation, because Partition had hit the farm sector hard.
Why not the others:
(A) Heavy industry was the thrust of the Second Plan (1956–61).
(C) Defence production was not a plan priority in the early 1950s.
(D) Information technology belongs to a much later period.
Key point: First Plan, agriculture; Second Plan, heavy industry.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Security in the Contemporary World
questions.sub_topic: Two freedoms in the broadest notion of human security
questions.question: The broadest notion of human security covers people's freedom from:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) want and fear
Why: Advocates of the broad view say human security means "freedom from want" and "freedom from fear": protection from hunger, disease and natural disasters as well as from violence.
Why not the others:
(A) Freedom from taxes is not a security concept.
(B) Conscription is a traditional defence issue.
(D) Trade and investment are economic questions, not human security.
Key point: Human security puts people, not states, at the centre.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Recent Issues and Challenges
questions.sub_topic: Prime Minister when the New Economic Policy began
questions.question: The New Economic Policy of 1991, which opened the Indian economy, was introduced when the Prime Minister was:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) P.V. Narasimha Rao
Why: The reforms began in 1991 under Prime Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao, with Manmohan Singh as Finance Minister.
Why not the others:
(B) Chandra Shekhar was Prime Minister until June 1991, before the reforms.
(C) V.P. Singh led the National Front government of 1989–90.
(D) Vajpayee's governments came later, from 1996 and 1998.
Key point: 1991, Rao and Manmohan Singh mark the start of liberalisation.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: End of the Soviet Union — the false claim
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The Soviet Union was made up of fifteen republics.
(B) In December 1991 Russia, Ukraine and Belarus announced the end of the USSR and formed the Commonwealth of Independent States.
(C) Russia took over the Soviet Union's seat in the UN Security Council.
(D) 'Shock therapy' was a slow, gradual transition to capitalism, favoured by the Communist Party.
Which of the statements given above is/are NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (D) only
Why: Only (D) is false: shock therapy was a sudden, total shift to capitalism, backed by the World Bank and the IMF, in which state assets were sold off quickly.
Why not the others: (A) the USSR had fifteen constituent republics, which became independent states. (B) the three republics declared the USSR's end and formed the CIS. (C) Russia was accepted as the USSR's successor state. Options (A), (B) and (C) name a true statement as false.
Key point: Shock therapy meant a rapid move to capitalism.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: South Asia in the Post-Cold War Era
questions.sub_topic: Neighbour whose king flushed out north-eastern militants
questions.question: Which neighbouring country's king helped India by flushing out guerrillas and militants from India's north-east who were operating from its territory?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Bhutan
Why: Bhutan's king undertook an operation to flush out militant groups from India's north-east that had bases in Bhutan. India is also involved in big hydroelectric projects there.
Why not the others:
(B) Nepal's relations with India have been strained at times over trade and Maoist activity.
(C) Myanmar is not a SAARC member.
(D) Bangladesh has disputes with India over water sharing and migration.
Key point: India and Bhutan have very close and cordial relations.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: Meaning of glasnost
questions.question: Gorbachev's policy of glasnost meant:
options: B) openness and freedom of expression
C) rapid privatisation of state assets
D) a military alliance with the West
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) openness and freedom of expression
Why: Glasnost meant openness, allowing criticism and freer discussion of the system.
Why not the others:
(A) Restructuring was perestroika.
(C) Rapid privatisation came later, under shock therapy.
(D) There was no military alliance with the West.
Key point: Glasnost is openness; perestroika is restructuring.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: South Asia in the Post-Cold War Era
questions.sub_topic: Military ruler who seized power in Pakistan in 1999
questions.question: Which army chief seized power in Pakistan in 1999?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) General Pervez Musharraf
Why: General Pervez Musharraf overthrew Nawaz Sharif's elected government in 1999. He became President in 2001.
Why not the others:
(A) Ayub Khan took over in 1958.
(B) Yahya Khan ruled during the 1971 crisis.
(C) Zia-ul-Haq seized power in 1977.
Key point: Pakistan alternated between army rule and elected governments.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Era of One-Party Dominance
questions.sub_topic: First non-Congress government formed through elections
questions.question: In 1957 the first government in India formed by a party other than the Congress through elections came to power in Kerala. Who led it?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) E.M.S. Namboodiripad
Why: The Communist Party of India won the 1957 Kerala Assembly election, and E.M.S. Namboodiripad became Chief Minister. The ministry was dismissed in 1959 under Article 356.
Why not the others:
(A) A.K. Gopalan was a Communist leader in Parliament, not the Chief Minister.
(B) Pattom Thanu Pillai of the Praja Socialist Party became Chief Minister in 1960, after the Communist ministry was dismissed.
(D) S.A. Dange was a Communist trade union leader.
Key point: Kerala 1957 was one of the first elected Communist governments in the world.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Globalisation and Its Critics
questions.sub_topic: Wearing jeans with a khadi kurta
questions.question: An Indian student wears blue jeans with a khadi kurta. According to NCERT, this mixing of an outside influence with a local tradition illustrates:
options: D) the death of local culture
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) cultural heterogenisation
Why: When outside influences mix with local traditions and create something new, globalisation broadens choices. This is cultural heterogenisation.
Why not the others:
(A) Homogenisation means one culture replacing all others.
(B) Cultural imperialism is the imposition of a dominant culture.
(D) Here the local tradition survives in a new combination.
Key point: Globalisation can enlarge cultural choices as well as narrow them.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Globalisation and Its Critics
questions.sub_topic: Indian city that hosted the World Social Forum
questions.question: Fill in the blank: The fourth meeting of the World Social Forum was held in ________ in 2004.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Mumbai
Why: The World Social Forum, an open meeting of groups opposed to neo-liberal globalisation, held its fourth meeting in Mumbai in January 2004.
Why not the others: (A), (C), (D) New Delhi, Kolkata and Chennai did not host the Forum.
Key point: Porto Alegre 2001, Mumbai 2004.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: Country that was NOT a founding member of ASEAN
questions.question: ASEAN was founded in 1967 by five countries. Which of the following was NOT one of them?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Vietnam
Why: The founders were Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand. Vietnam joined in 1995.
Why not the others: (A), (B), (C) Indonesia, Singapore and Thailand all signed the Bangkok Declaration of 1967.
Key point: The five founders: Indonesia, Malaysia, Philippines, Singapore, Thailand.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Security in the Contemporary World
questions.sub_topic: Arms-control treaties in order
questions.question:
Arrange the following arms-control agreements in chronological order of signing:
(A) The Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty
(B) The Chemical Weapons Convention
(C) The Biological Weapons Convention
(D) START I
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (C), (D), (B)
Why: (A) The NPT was signed in 1968. (C) The BWC followed in 1972. (D) START I was signed in 1991. (B) The CWC was signed in 1992.
Why not the others: Option (B) puts the BWC before the NPT. Option (C) puts the CWC before START I. Option (D) puts START I before the BWC.
Key point: NPT 1968, BWC 1972, START I 1991, CWC 1992.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Disintegration of the 'Second World' and the Collapse of Bipolarity
questions.sub_topic: Country that is NOT a Central Asian republic
questions.question: Which of the following countries, all of which emerged from the Soviet Union, is NOT a Central Asian republic?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Georgia
Why: Georgia lies in the Caucasus, between the Black Sea and the Caspian, not in Central Asia.
Why not the others: (B), (C), (D) Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Kyrgyzstan, with Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, are the five Central Asian republics.
Key point: The Central Asian five all end in "-stan".

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: What the 'ASEAN Way' means
questions.question: The 'ASEAN Way' refers to:
options: A) an informal, non-confrontational and cooperative style of interaction
B) a single common currency adopted by all of the ASEAN member countries
C) a supranational parliament whose laws bind every one of the member states
D) a formal military alliance of the members directed against China
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) an informal, non-confrontational and cooperative style of interaction
Why: ASEAN members value informal, non-confrontational and cooperative interaction, with respect for national sovereignty.
Why not the others:
(B) ASEAN has no common currency, unlike the Euro area.
(C) ASEAN has no supranational parliament; that is closer to the EU model.
(D) ASEAN is not a military alliance.
Key point: The ASEAN Way avoids confrontation and respects sovereignty.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: India's External Relations
questions.sub_topic: Why India signed the 1971 treaty with the Soviet Union
questions.question: In August 1971 India signed a 20-year Treaty of Peace and Friendship with the Soviet Union. What was the main reason?
options: A) To join the Soviet-led Warsaw Pact and host Soviet troops on Indian soil
B) To be assured of Soviet support if attacked, as the US and China backed Pakistan
C) To obtain Soviet scientists and fuel for the first nuclear test at Pokhran
D) To leave the Non-Aligned Movement and follow Soviet foreign policy
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) To be assured of Soviet support if attacked, as the US and China backed Pakistan
Why: During the East Pakistan crisis, an alignment of the US and China behind Pakistan was taking shape. The 1971 treaty assured India of Soviet support if it was attacked.
Why not the others:
(A) India never joined the Warsaw Pact.
(C) The 1974 test was India's own programme.
(D) India remained a leading member of NAM.
Key point: The 1971 treaty balanced the US–China–Pakistan alignment.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: Alternative Centres of Economic and Political Power
questions.sub_topic: Founding dates in the rise of new centres of power
questions.question:
Match List-I (Event) with List-II (Year).

List-I
(A) Formation of ASEAN
(B) Formation of the ASEAN Regional Forum
(C) Signing of the Maastricht Treaty
(D) China's entry into the WTO

List-II
(I) 1967
(II) 2001
(III) 1994
(IV) 1992
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(I), (B)-(III), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)
Why: ASEAN was set up in 1967 by the Bangkok Declaration (I). The ASEAN Regional Forum was set up in 1994 (III). The Maastricht Treaty created the European Union in 1992 (IV). China joined the WTO in 2001 (II).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps 1992 and 1994. Option (B) puts ASEAN's formation in 1994. Option (D) puts Maastricht in 2001.
Key point: ASEAN 1967, ARF 1994, EU 1992, China in the WTO 2001.

questions.topic: Contemporary World Politics: International Organisations in a Unipolar World
questions.sub_topic: Nature of Amnesty International
questions.question: Amnesty International is:
options: A) a specialised agency of the United Nations based in Geneva
B) a regional trade bloc of developing countries in Asia and Africa
C) a military alliance of Western states formed after the Cold War
D) a non-governmental organisation that campaigns for human rights
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) a non-governmental organisation that campaigns for human rights
Why: Amnesty International is an NGO that campaigns for human rights around the world and publishes reports on abuses.
Why not the others:
(A) It is not a UN agency; it is independent of governments.
(B) It has nothing to do with trade.
(C) It is not an alliance of states.
Key point: NGOs are new non-state actors in global governance.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Nation-Building and Its Problems
questions.sub_topic: The Nizam's paramilitary force in Hyderabad
questions.question: Fill in the blank: The Nizam of Hyderabad's paramilitary force, which attacked people opposed to the Nizam's rule in 1948, was known as the ________.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Razakars
Why: The Razakars were the Nizam's paramilitary force. Their violence against the people's movement in Hyderabad was followed by the Indian Army's action in September 1948.
Why not the others:
(A) The Khudai Khidmatgars were Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan's non-violent volunteers.
(B) The Ghadarites were revolutionaries of the Ghadar movement abroad.
(D) "Redshirts" was another name for the Khudai Khidmatgars.
Key point: Razakars, the Nizam and 1948 go together.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Challenge to and Restoration of Congress System
questions.sub_topic: Events from Shastri to 'Garibi Hatao' in order
questions.question:
Arrange the following events in chronological order:
(A) The Lok Sabha election fought on the slogan 'Garibi Hatao'
(B) Nationalisation of fourteen private banks
(C) Lal Bahadur Shastri becomes Prime Minister
(D) The fourth general election
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (C), (D), (B), (A)
Why: (C) Shastri became Prime Minister in June 1964. (D) The fourth general election was held in February 1967. (B) Fourteen banks were nationalised in July 1969. (A) The 'Garibi Hatao' election was held in March 1971.
Why not the others: Option (A) puts bank nationalisation before 1967. Option (B) puts the 1967 election before Shastri's succession. Option (C) puts the 1971 election before bank nationalisation.
Key point: 1964 → 1967 → 1969 → 1971 traces the Congress's fall and recovery.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Nation-Building and Its Problems
questions.sub_topic: States reorganisation in the 1950s — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The States Reorganisation Commission was appointed in 1953.
(B) The States Reorganisation Act of 1956 created 14 States and 6 Union Territories.
(C) The death of Potti Sriramulu after a long fast forced the government to announce a separate Andhra State in 1952.
(D) Gujarat and Maharashtra were created by the States Reorganisation Act of 1956.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A) the Commission was set up in 1953 to look into redrawing State boundaries. (B) its report led to the 1956 Act, which created 14 States and 6 Union Territories. (C) Sriramulu died in December 1952 after a 56-day fast, and the Prime Minister then announced a separate Andhra State.
Why not the others: (D) is false: Bombay State was split into Gujarat and Maharashtra only in 1960. Options (C) and (D) include (D); option (B) leaves out (C).
Key point: Linguistic reorganisation began with Andhra and continued well after 1956.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Crises of the Constitutional Order
questions.sub_topic: Constitutional provision used for the 1975 Emergency
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

In June 1975 the Allahabad High Court set aside Indira Gandhi's election to the Lok Sabha on an election petition filed by Raj Narain, her rival in the 1971 contest. The Supreme Court granted a partial stay: she could remain a member but could not vote in Parliament until her appeal was decided. Opposition parties, led by Jayaprakash Narayan, called for nationwide protests and asked the army, the police and government employees not to obey "illegal and immoral orders". On the night of 25 June 1975 the government advised the President to declare an emergency on the ground of "internal disturbance". The Constitution allowed this, and the declaration concentrated power in the Union government. Newspapers were censored, many opposition leaders were arrested under preventive detention laws, some organisations were banned and the right to approach the courts for the protection of fundamental rights was suspended. Parliament also passed a series of constitutional amendments. In January 1977 elections were announced, and after the Janata Party's victory a commission of inquiry was set up to examine the excesses committed during this period.

Question: Under which Article of the Constitution was the emergency described in the passage declared on the ground of "internal disturbance"?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Article 352
Why: Article 352 provides for a national emergency on the ground of war, external aggression or (as it then read) "internal disturbance". The 1975 declaration invoked internal disturbance.
Why not the others:
(A) Article 356 is President's Rule in a single State, used in Kerala in 1959.
(C) Article 360 is the financial emergency, never declared.
(D) Article 368 is the procedure for amending the Constitution.
Key point: National emergency is Article 352; State emergency is Article 356.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Crises of the Constitutional Order
questions.sub_topic: Date on which the national emergency was declared
questions.question:

In January 1977 elections were announced, and after the Janata Party's victory a commission of inquiry was set up to examine the excesses committed during this period.

Question: On which date was the emergency described in the passage declared?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 25 June 1975
Why: The President proclaimed the emergency on the night of 25 June 1975, on the government's advice; the passage dates it directly.
Why not the others:
(A) 12 June 1975 is the date of the Allahabad High Court verdict that preceded it.
(B) 26 January 1976 is unconnected; the emergency was then in force.
(C) January 1977 is when fresh elections were announced.
Key point: Verdict 12 June, emergency 25 June 1975, elections March 1977.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Crises of the Constitutional Order
questions.sub_topic: Who filed the election petition against Indira Gandhi
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

The Supreme Court granted a partial stay: she could remain a member but could not vote in Parliament until her appeal was decided. Opposition parties, led by Jayaprakash Narayan, called for nationwide protests and asked the army, the police and government employees not to obey "illegal and immoral orders". Question: The election petition that led to the Allahabad High Court verdict described in the passage was filed by:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Raj Narain
Why: Raj Narain, a socialist leader who had lost to Indira Gandhi in Rae Bareli in 1971, challenged her election; the court set it aside in June 1975.
Why not the others:
(B) Jayaprakash Narayan led the protest movement, not the petition.
(C) Morarji Desai became Prime Minister after the 1977 election.
(D) George Fernandes led the 1974 railway strike.
Key point: The petition was Raj Narain's; the movement was JP's.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Crises of the Constitutional Order
questions.sub_topic: Commission that inquired into the excesses of the Emergency
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Question: The commission of inquiry mentioned at the end of the passage, set up in 1977 to examine the excesses of the emergency, was headed by:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Justice J.C. Shah
Why: The Janata government appointed the Shah Commission, headed by retired Supreme Court judge J.C. Shah, in May 1977.
Why not the others:
(A) A.N. Ray was made Chief Justice in 1973 by superseding three senior judges.
(B) Jagmohan Lal Sinha was the Allahabad High Court judge who decided the election case.
(C) B.P. Mandal chaired the Second Backward Classes Commission and was not a judge.
Key point: Shah Commission, 1977, for the excesses of the Emergency.

questions.topic: Politics in India since Independence: Crises of the Constitutional Order
questions.sub_topic: Which was NOT a feature of the emergency period
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

In June 1975 the Allahabad High Court set aside Indira Gandhi's election to the Lok Sabha on an election petition filed by Raj Narain, her rival in the 1971 contest. The Supreme Court granted a partial stay: she could remain a member but could not vote in Parliament until her appeal was decided. Opposition parties, led by Jayaprakash Narayan, called for nationwide protests and asked the army, the police and government employees not to obey "illegal and immoral orders". On the night of 25 June 1975 the government advised the President to declare an emergency on the ground of "internal disturbance". The Constitution allowed this, and the declaration concentrated power in the Union government. Newspapers were censored, many opposition leaders were arrested under preventive detention laws, some organisations were banned and the right to approach the courts for the protection of fundamental rights was suspended. Parliament also passed a series of constitutional amendments. In January 1977 elections were announced, and after the Janata Party's victory a commission of inquiry was set up to examine the excesses committed during this period.

Question: Based on the passage and your knowledge of the period, which of the following was NOT a feature of the emergency of 1975–77?
options: B) Arrest of opposition leaders under preventive detention
C) Lok Sabha elections held as scheduled in early 1976
D) Suspension of the right to move courts for fundamental rights
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Lok Sabha elections held as scheduled in early 1976
Why: Elections due in 1976 were postponed; the Lok Sabha's term was extended, and fresh elections were held only in March 1977.
Why not the others:
(A) The passage states that newspapers were censored.
(B) Preventive detention was used widely against opposition leaders.
(D) The passage notes that the right to approach the courts was suspended.
Key point: The emergency postponed elections; the 1977 election ended it.
